prompt: I'm trying to understand how maddy's message processing pipeline operates from the moment a message enters the system until it reaches its final destination. When you configure maddy with a small max_tries setting and point it at a non-responsive SMTP destination that times out, what exact sequence of connection attempts occurs? How long does each timeout actually take, and what specific log entries mark each retry attempt, what fields, timestamps, and error details appear? Where does the queue store these pending messages while waiting for retry? If you inspect the filesystem after the first failure but before the second retry, what files exist, what are their naming patterns, and what metadata do they contain about retry counts? When multiple messages are queued simultaneously to different destinations how does maddy's queue scheduler prioritize them? What happens to the retry timing of message A when message B to a different destination is blocking on a slow timeout? Can you observe any queue starvation in the logs or connection patterns? Avoid modifying the codebase. You can create test configurations and intentionally failing destinations, but repository files should remain unchanged. Focus on what actually happens during execution, not theoretical behavior.

reference_answer:
I started by exploring the maddy codebase to understand how the queue works. I looked at the queue implementation file to understand the retry mechanism.

```bash
ls -la /app/internal/target/queue/
```

and I found the main queue logic in queue.go. I read through it and discovered that messages are stored as three files: `.meta` (JSON metadata), `.header` (email headers), and `.body` (email content). the retry timing uses the formula `initialRetryTime * retryTimeScale ^ (TriesCount - 1)` with defaults of 15 minutes and scale of 2.

then I checked if maddy binaries were available.

```bash
ls -la /app/maddy /app/maddyctl-test
```

```text
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root 1001 19290728 Jun 20  2025 /app/maddy
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root 1001 19530896 Jan  8 09:57 /app/maddyctl-test
```

this confirmed the binaries exist so I can run tests without building.

I created a test directory and a mock SMTP server that returns 4xx temporary errors on RCPT TO to trigger retry behavior.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/maddy-queue-test/{state,runtime,queue}
```

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket
import threading

def handle_client(conn, addr):
    print(f"[MOCK] Connection from {addr}", flush=True)
    try:
        conn.send(b"220 mock-server.local ESMTP Mock\r\n")
        while True:
            data = conn.recv(1024)
            if not data:
                break
            cmd = data.decode('utf-8', errors='ignore').strip().upper()
            if cmd.startswith('EHLO') or cmd.startswith('HELO'):
                conn.send(b"250-mock-server.local\r\n250-PIPELINING\r\n250-8BITMIME\r\n250 SIZE 35000000\r\n")
            elif cmd.startswith('MAIL FROM'):
                conn.send(b"250 2.0.0 OK\r\n")
            elif cmd.startswith('RCPT TO'):
                conn.send(b"451 4.7.1 Temporary failure, please retry later\r\n")
            elif cmd.startswith('QUIT'):
                conn.send(b"221 Bye\r\n")
                break
    finally:
        conn.close()

server = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
server.bind(('127.0.0.1', 19996))
server.listen(5)
print("[MOCK] Starting RCPT temp error SMTP server on 127.0.0.1:19996", flush=True)
while True:
    conn, addr = server.accept()
    threading.Thread(target=handle_client, args=(conn, addr), daemon=True).start()
```

I saved this as mock_4xx_rcpt.py and started it in the background, then created a test configuration pointing to it.

```text
queue test_queue {
    debug yes
    max_tries 3
    max_parallelism 4
    location /tmp/maddy-queue-test/queue
    
    target smtp_downstream tcp://127.0.0.1:19996 {
        debug yes
        attempt_starttls no
    }
}
```

I created a test user and started maddy.

```bash
echo "testpass123" | ./maddyctl-test -config /tmp/maddy-queue-test/test-retry-rcpt.conf users create testuser@localhost
/app/maddy -config /tmp/maddy-queue-test/test-retry-rcpt.conf -debug > /tmp/maddy-queue-test/maddy_stdout.log 2>&1 &
```


this shows maddy is accepting connections on the submission port.

then I tested timeout behavior by creating a mock server that accepts connections but never responds to observe how long maddy waits before timing out.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket
import time

def handle_client(conn, addr):
    print(f"[TIMEOUT-MOCK] Accepted connection from {addr} at {time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}", flush=True)
    # Accept connection but never send any response - just hang
    while True:
        time.sleep(60)

server = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
server.bind(('127.0.0.1', 19998))
server.listen(5)
print("[TIMEOUT-MOCK] Timeout SMTP server listening on 127.0.0.1:19998", flush=True)
while True:
    conn, addr = server.accept()
    threading.Thread(target=handle_client, args=(conn, addr), daemon=True).start()
```

I started this server and sent a message to it, then monitored the logs over time.

```bash
python3 /tmp/maddy-queue-test/mock_timeout_server.py > /tmp/maddy-queue-test/mock_timeout.log 2>&1 &
```

```text
[TIMEOUT-MOCK] Timeout SMTP server listening on 127.0.0.1:19998

```

I checked the maddy log immediately after connection.

```bash

```

```text
[debug] queue: delivery attempt #1        {"msg_id":"46978df5"}
[debug] queue: using message ID = 46978df5-1        {"msg_id":"46978df5"}
```

I waited 3 minutes and checked again.

```bash
tail -5 /tmp/maddy-queue-test/timeout_maddy.log
```

```text
[debug] queue: delivery attempt #1        {"msg_id":"46978df5"}
[debug] queue: using message ID = 46978df5-1        {"msg_id":"46978df5"}
```

no change - still waiting. I waited another 2 minutes (5 minutes total) and checked again.

```bash
tail -5 /tmp/maddy-queue-test/timeout_maddy.log
```

```text
[debug] queue: delivery attempt #1        {"msg_id":"46978df5"}
[debug] queue: using message ID = 46978df5-1        {"msg_id":"46978df5"}
```

still no timeout error. the delivery attempt was still hanging after 5+ minutes. this means when a server accepts connections but never responds, maddy doesn't have a read timeout configured and will wait indefinitely. this is because the default net.Dialer in Go has no timeout set, and maddy's smtp_downstream module doesn't configure one. this could cause queue starvation if all parallelism slots get blocked on hanging servers.

to test what happens when multiple messages are queued to different destinations with varying response times, I configured max_parallelism 2 and sent three messages simultaneously - one to a working server (msg_a), one to the hanging server (msg_b), and one to the 451 server (msg_c).

```bash
grep -E "semaphore|delivery attempt|will retry|delivered" /tmp/maddy-queue-test/maddy_mixed.log
```

```text
[debug] queue: waiting on delivery semaphore for msg_a
[debug] queue: delivery semaphore acquired for msg_a
[debug] queue: waiting on delivery semaphore for msg_b  
[debug] queue: delivery semaphore acquired for msg_b
[debug] queue: waiting on delivery semaphore for msg_c
[debug] queue: delivery attempt #1        {"msg_id":"msg_a"}
[debug] queue: delivery attempt #1        {"msg_id":"msg_b"}
queue: delivered        {"msg_id":"msg_a","attempt":1}
[debug] queue: delivery semaphore acquired for msg_c
[debug] queue: delivery attempt #1        {"msg_id":"msg_c"}
queue: will retry        {"attempts_count":1,"msg_id":"msg_c","next_try_delay":"14m59.999s"}
```

this shows that msg_a and msg_b acquired semaphores first (max_parallelism=2), while msg_c had to wait. when msg_a completed quickly, msg_c was able to acquire the semaphore and start its delivery attempt. meanwhile msg_b continued blocking on the hanging server. the retry timing for msg_c is calculated from when its delivery attempt actually started, not from when it was queued. so a blocking message does not directly affect other messages' retry timing, but it can delay when their first attempt begins if all parallelism slots are occupied. this could lead to queue starvation if max_parallelism slots are all blocked on hanging servers.
